front: Entropy?
back: A measure of the dispersal of matter and energy; S(gas) ≫ S(liquid) > S(solid).

front: When is ΔS positive?
back: More moles of gas, melting/boiling/dissolving, rising temperature.

front: ΔS⦵ from data?
back: ΣS⦵(products) − ΣS⦵(reactants), J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

front: Gibbs equation and spontaneity?
back: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; spontaneous if ΔG < 0.

front: Temperature at which ΔG = 0?
back: T = ΔH/ΔS (same units: kJ and kJ K⁻¹).

front: ΔG⦵ and K?
back: ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K. Negative ΔG⦵ → K > 1.

front: Spontaneous (thermodynamically favourable) reaction?
back: One that proceeds in the stated direction without continuous external energy input; ΔG < 0. Says nothing about rate.

front: Does a negative ΔG mean a reaction is fast?
back: No. ΔG predicts feasibility only; a large Ea can make it immeasurably slow (e.g. diamond → graphite).

front: Why are standard entropies of elements not zero?
back: Entropy is absolute: only a perfect crystal at 0 K has S = 0, so all substances at 298 K have positive S⦵ (unlike ΔHf⦵).

front: Factors that increase the entropy of a substance?
back: Gas > liquid > solid; higher temperature; more complex molecules (more atoms); mixing/dissolving.

front: Sign of ΔS for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g)?
back: Negative: 4 mol of gas become 2 mol of gas (fewer ways to disperse energy and matter).

front: Unit trap in ΔG = ΔH − TΔS?
back: ΔH is in kJ mol⁻¹ but ΔS in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: divide ΔS by 1000 before combining. T in K.

front: Spontaneity for the four sign combinations of ΔH and ΔS?
back: −,+: always spontaneous. +,−: never. −,−: spontaneous at low T. +,+: spontaneous at high T.

front: ΔG⦵ from standard Gibbs energies of formation?
back: ΔG⦵ = ΣΔGf⦵(products) − ΣΔGf⦵(reactants); ΔGf⦵ of elements in their standard states is zero.

front: How does ΔG relate to total entropy?
back: ΔS(surroundings) = −ΔH/T, so ΔG = −TΔS(total); ΔG < 0 means total entropy increases (second law).

front: Graph of ΔG against T?
back: Straight line: gradient = −ΔS, y-intercept = ΔH; it crosses ΔG = 0 at T = ΔH/ΔS.

front: Value of ΔG at equilibrium and what ΔG⦵ tells you?
back: ΔG = 0 at equilibrium. ΔG⦵ < 0 → K > 1 (products favoured); ΔG⦵ > 0 → K < 1.

front: Calculating K from ΔG⦵?
back: K = e^(−ΔG⦵/RT), with ΔG⦵ in J mol⁻¹, R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and T in K.

front: Why does NH₄NO₃ dissolve spontaneously though endothermic?
back: Dissolving increases entropy greatly (ions dispersed), so TΔS > ΔH and ΔG < 0.

front: Why do reactions stop at equilibrium instead of going to completion?
back: Gibbs energy of the mixture reaches a minimum at the equilibrium composition (mixing of reactants and products lowers G).
